newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians clash with police, town hall on fire.
newsitem.headline: Albanians clash with police, town hall on fire.

text.p: Thousands of irate Albanians, facing the loss of their life savings in pyramid investment schemes, clashed with riot police Tirana on Sunday and called on the right-wing government to resign.

Violence also erupted in the town of Vlore, 150 km (95 miles) south of Tirana, where protesters set fire to the town hall. The crowd forced their way past an army unit on the scene but there no reports of clashes.
Eyewitnesses said they heard explosions, but this could not be confirmed independently.
By 1200 GMT the throng in Tirana's Skanderbeg Square, scene of anti-government demonstrations last year, had swollen to around 30,000, witnesses said.
Between 1,000 and 2,000 demonstrators, who had joined an opposition rally numbering in a central soccer stadium, broke away after the meeting ended and ran straight into a wall of riot police.
"People hurled stones, pushing back riot police as they tried to head towards the Martyrs of the Nation boulevard (leading off Skanderbeg Square)," a witness said.
Eyewitnesses told Reuters the police seemed reluctant to counter the barrage of stones but the situation was tense.

The protests, which began nearly two weeks ago, have gathered momentum across the Balkan country, Europe's poorest, as desperate people have seen their life savings evaporate with the collapse of some pyramid schemes.
Many Albanians blame the government of President Sali Berisha for failing to regulate the schemes and using them for its own gain.
Pyramid investment schemes, luring investors with promises of high returns on small outlay, have mushroomed in Albania since the fall of communism in 1990.

Troops were guarding state buildings in the southern town of Berat after the town hall was set ablaze on Saturday. Protesters also set fire to the town hall in Lushnje, southwest of Tirana, on Friday night.
On Saturday in Lushnje, a jeering crowd of 5,000 attacked Foreign Minister and ruling Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu, who was injured in the skirmish.
Opposition leaders at Sunday soccer stadium rally in the capital denounced the government for allegedly exploiting the schemes for its own gain.
"It is not the pyramid schemes which have gone bankrupt but Berisha's pyramid of power," Social Democrat leader Skender Gjinushi told the crowd.
In a televised address, embattled Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi promised his government would start paying back savers' deposits from February onwards.

"With the preparations made so far we may start the systematic distribution of the money from about February 5," Meksi said, adding the government already had a stockpile of 30 billion leks ($300 million) from two pyramid schemes.
But the pledge did little to quell the unrest.

"We shall overthrow the government today at all costs," one protester at the stadium said, adding there were rumours the Democratic Party used money from pyramid schemes to fund their election campaign last summer.
